I was using Opus via Cursor, did an audit with Gemini 3.1 Pro, Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4. Then I asked Opus to give assessment of the audit quality (anonymously). And I think it 100% nailed the current state of the models:
Gemini 3.1 Pro: The weakest. Looked at the screen. Found the obvious scale issues, confirmed previous fixes landed, but missed the wrong counts, dead sync buttons, inert controls, and radar state mismatches. A spot-check, not an audit.
Opus 4.6: The most precise. Read the code. Pinpointed the sanitizer fallback with exact line numbers and surfaced the systemic session-persistence problem -- the best single insight across all three audits. But never called the endpoints or tested whether controls actually do what they claim.
GPT-5.4-xHigh: The most thorough. Ran the code. Hit sync endpoints at runtime, compared rebuild state against legacy route snapshots field by field, and traced control bindings from declaration through to renderer. The only auditor that verified the full chain end to end.

- Taste / judgement
- Training or hard to validate tasks
- Real-time interactions
- Learning
- Self-critique & self-healing
- Manipulating documents
- Entity with persistence & liability
I can't predict if some of these will be AGI-level this year or they'll stay 'hacky' another 3-5 years. This creates very different futures and implications for the job market & AI usefulness.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
I'm very curious about OpenAI's planned intern researcher release by September this year. Having tried using current LLMs for OpenAI's Golf Challenge, I would say that Codex & Opus are actively bad researchers (not meaningful difference between them)
- They come up with small ideas anchored to what we have - they find it hard to step back and try another route
- They set up bad experiments with fallbacks other cheats
- They are terrible judges at what is actually meaningful - every idea is rated 9/10 and then nothing works
Bear in mind that some of these things are not too bad in the land of software, e.g. in software you do want reasonable fallbacks, you do want to build something that works that might mean a smaller iteration rather than tearing the whole thing down.
But for research (even in a small sense, e.g. tuning a prompt) - this is really bad. I want the models to be genuinely stepping back and assessing if they are barking up the wrong tree. I want them to design clean experiments that don't muddy the water with dumb fallbacks that make it seem like something is working.
It doesn't feel obvious to me that you could easily have a single LLM (in the short term at least) that could be a great software engineer and a great researcher. I'm sure we'll get there at some point, but I'd best that the research intern would feel quite different to Codex, if it would actually be good at research.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Open source vs proprietary race: the key point here, is that gap between open source and proprietary models was fairly large (100-150 points), then proprietary models fumbled around so the gap narrowed to c.50 pts, then the 50 point gap remained for over a year, so no clear 'catching up' by open source models in the recent past - about steady gap remains.
Quoting @arena
Are open source models catching up to proprietary models? We’ve looked back at 3 years of Arena’s data to show how the race has evolved.
For comparison, we’ve taken the top 20% of the models and uncovered the following:
- Before mid 2024: The gap was between 100-150 points
- In the second half of 2024, the gap rapidly narrowed to ~50 points
- This was driven by the fact that proprietary models have not significantly improved between early 2023 and November 2024 - hovering around the 1350 score for the top 20% of proprietary models
- Then since Jan 2025, we saw a parallel improvement in both proprietary and open source models
- Meaning that for the last ~14 months the gap stayed steady at around 50-60 points
For context, 50 points is the gap between the 1st and 20th place in the Overall leaderboard
Today, proprietary models take up the first 20 spots on the Text Arena, with @AnthropicAI, @GoogleDeepMind , @xai and @OpenAI leading in the rankings.
The top open source models are ranked #20 (GLM-5 by @Zai_org ), #23 (Kimi-K2.5-Thinking by @Kimi_Moonshot ) and #27 (Qwen3.5-397b-a17b by @Alibaba_Qwen ).

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Famously, the only measurable impact of automating horses with cars was saving on hay and vet bills
Quoting @levie
The thing that most people miss initially with agents is that the scope of what we will produce will go up commensurate with what the tools can now automate, which basically means we’ll working the same or even more.
Everyone thinks that we will use AI to do what we already do but cheaper and faster, which would lead to fewer people or getting more time back. In fact it will just mean we’re doing more things.
Once we figured out that we can automate a particular task, you then expand the size of work to do many more of those or other tasks in a project. The result is that you’re actually combining many other previously hard to combine tasks into a single workflow, causing even more work.
The software project scope now multiplies because you know you can build far more. The customer insights project now balloons because you know you can reasonably aggregate far more data. The marketing campaign has even more creative production because it’s cheaper and easier.
This is going to happen in almost every field of work.

Four months on, I must say that ALL of the ChatGPT android app issues I listed are fixed. The biggest win is that I don't need to keep the 'thinking' tab alive - it removes to much mental load.
Lots of silent updates & fixes - lovely work @nickaturley & the team
Quoting @petergostev
My problems with ChatGPT for any PMs looking what to do during the 'code red' situation (long list just features, not models, android user, pro subscriber):
Android app has really deteriorated:
- Android app takes several seconds to remember what model I used before, so I end up sending simple queries to Pro or hard queries to Auto all the time
- When sharing the image to the android app it doesn't attach in a way that uses vision, but instead it does OCR with python. I need to attach image from the chat for it to work
- Thinking doesn't work in the background like pro, why do I need to keep my chat active for minutes at a time?
- Pro doesn't send notifications half the time when it's done - I've got so many dead queries that I sent and forgot I did
- Constant weirdness with connection - I never know if things are done or not, sometimes things break and no response given
- is the response done? To check I need to refresh, but to refresh I need to go to all charts and drag it from there rather than in the chat
- I still can't manage tasks from the app, I have some going back a year that I forget to switch off
Web app & other:
- what happened to canvas? It was a nice feature no preview button stopped working and it is a buggy mess
- Custom GPTs is a nice feature for business but it has no love for the last 2 years and that whole line has died out - non technical users are not vibe coding, they have nothing else 2 years on. Agent builder is not in chatgpt and is hard to use for non technical people
- voice is transcription is not reliable apart from short recordings, probably the connection issue again, I'm too afraid to use it after losing several minutes of voice notes
- the whole connection issue and thinking not giving outputs is just abysmal, it has to get better
- data analyst is still very janky - you can upload only limited files, it breaks half the time, it is a huge use case for business but non-Codex users are stuck in 2023. I'm basically recommending people don't use chatgpt for data analysis anymore
- we are still stuck with different experiences depending on what file you upload how, you need to be an expert in knowing how chatgpt treats different files to use it properly
- I don't use the mac app that much but understand it is behind on many features now (eg group chats)
That's everything I could think of now. I know AI is fast moving and it is hard to keep everything going. And maybe I'm a dumb android user and things are better on the other side, but I hope the 'code red' won't be just get another model iteration out but actually go back to caring about the core ChatGPT experience

summary:
Compute Wars: OpenAI vs Anthopic.
Why was Opus 4.5 such a breakthrough? Anthropic got lots more compute from AWS Madison and New Carlisle sites likely more than doubling their capacity.
This got Anthropic got close to OpenAI's total capacity, and probably much higher effective capacity available for new model runs.
Remember that it takes 6+ months between getting capacity and releasing the model, so the extra OpenAI capacity might be aligning well with the 'spud' model rather than GPT-5.4.
Unless something dramatic happens, OpenAI will pull away in terms of compute available in H2 2026, but 2027 will be close. Future years are less certain but so far OpenAI has much higher planned capacity, though can't imagine Anthropic isn't pushing as hard as they can to get lots more compute.
Always watch the compute, other things matter, but any new capability breakthrough probably came from throwing more compute at it.

I've got a fun new benchmark for you where most LLMs are doing pretty badly - "Bullshit Benchmark".
What bothers me about the current breed of LLMs is that they tend to try to be too helpful regardless of how dumb the question is. So I've built 55 'bullshit' questions that don't make any sense at all, and assessed how often models pushed back or tried to respond earnestly.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Significant downside of larger models is that it is much harder to do RL on them. Smaller model = quicker RL cycles, bigger model = slower RL cycles.
So far this matches - GPT-5 is the smallest model with quickest iterations, Gemini 3 is biggest and slowest iterations, Claude is in between. I'm sure size is not the only factor, but it matters.
That might be the downside of Mythos - it looks like a chonk, so any further RL on it would be slower than a smaller model. So a bull case for OpenAI is that while Spud likely starts off being worse than Mythos, but sine it is likely smaller, it catches up & overtakes by the 2nd or 3rd iteration through more rapid RL cycles.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
A good start-up idea is to take any popular app and make an extremely agent-friendly version of it - sort of an 'agent arbitrage'.
Slack, Workday, Notion, Figma, Navan etc. are all very clunky with agents, even if they have an agent/MCP, they are nowhere good enough.
I am now getting to a point where I can't imagine doing things 'by hand' anymore. I needed to put a photo album together and I was seriously thinking if I could somehow hook an agent up to do it for me. I decided to bite the bullet and spend half an hour on this task vs 3 hours hooking up the agent, but this is a one off.
Heavy agent users will start getting annoyed with apps that aren't agent friendly and will happily churn to something that is. Who knows how long this will last, but in the short term there's a lot of 'agent arbitrage' to be had, as established apps don't want to undermine their business.

A common problem we will now see is the kind of 'google disease' but at mass scale. Where smart engineers can ship apps quickly, then lose interest and move on to something else cool to ship. It feels good to ship a whole new app, but less cool to keep fixing bugs a year later.
Quoting @theo
I feel bad dunking on them so much but it's genuinely absurd how bad the new Claude Code desktop app is. You can feel the vibe code leaking everywhere.
Every "feature" is barely integrated and full of edge cases that weren't considered. Every menu feels barren, stuffed in last second for some random toggle. Every hotkey breaks as soon as you try to do anything else.
I've lost track of how many bugs I've encountered. I found at least 40 in under an hour. And it's all truly absurd arcane shit. Stuff like voice mode typing in all input boxes instead of just the one you have focused.
Any one of these issues would have been enough for me to do a massive post-mortem and likely fire someone. A $400b company shipping this is absurd.
I feel like I'm going mad. How does anyone seriously use this?? It is broken on fundamental levels that are hard to comprehend.
How are we supposed to trust the code these models produce if Anthropic's official showcases are absolute slop?

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
GPT Image 2 + Codex: or how to make Codex not suck at UI.
Step 1: Generate a UI image (native in Codex)
Step 2: Get Codex to implement the UI based on it
Step 3: Get Codex to iterate until it aligns with the image as much as possible
Codex is bad at initial UI, but very good at implementing a reference design, so this is your way out - iterate with the image model first and then Codex will do a good job.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
PSA: High (4k) vs Low (1k) quality: both are not bad, but if you zoom in, the high quality has substantially more detail and no errors, while the low quality very notesable issues with text rendering.
ChatGPT itself has another layer of complexity for Thinking, but these are generated on the API Playground with the Quality and Size settings changed.
If you you need more control for higher quality outputs, I highly recommend using higher settings via the API. Low is still good, but not as good as High for sure.
4k can also enhance quality beyond the obvious, the actual generation could be better. This is not equivalent to a mechanical upscaling. I am not sure why, but more pixels=more tokens=better output is not a bad heuristic.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Opus 4.7 - 400k vs 1m context - is there a difference?
I've heard @theo talk about the fact that it is unlikely that Anthropic would have offered up a model with 1m context at the same cost, if it wasn't a different (i.e. cheaper to serve) model.
I did a test where I toggled the 1m default model on & off in Claude Code (otherwise default settings, xHigh reasoning) and compared the outputs with 3x generations - same prompts etc.
My observations:
- Models feel DIFFERENT - often when you ask a model for the same generation, you get a somewhat different answer, but it feels & smells the same. Here 400k and 1m are very different every time
- 400k model seems better - not that 1m is trash and 400k is amazing, but there are definitely issues with the level of ambition and accuracy that 1m model seems to have
Examples of 1m failing:
- Voxel Rome: the colosseum is nowhere near as impressive
- Golden Gate: cars go sideways, waves not very high, bridge goes into land; though the structure of the bridge is a bit better
- Stonehenge: structure is more 'wrong', lighting, shadows & textures are more flat and not as rich
This isn't a conclusive evidence of course, but at least to me the two models do not behave the same way. Anecdotally as well when building 1m felt like it was doing more weird validation (e.g. going around in circles) and 400k was more straightforward. These sorts of things are harder to capture in tests, but you'd notice in Claude Code.
You can review the hosted generations, see the code & prompts in the links below
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2049231054150782976/img/_bObRisqfA0ciw_w.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2049231054150782976/vid/avc1/320x350/VMiLRxOa7jF9PzAU.mp4?tag=21

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
I know everything is a skill issue, but I didn't have a good experience with /goal in Codex CLI. I tried giving it 2 tasks, that were hard but well specified.
1) Build a video stabiliser on top of open source to match the Google Photos stabiliser in quality.
I had a starter and a reference video and a pretty good spec prepared with Codex ahead of time. It spent I think 24h+ hours and the output originally was just bad, but then with some steering got to an OK point but not materially better than the open source start. Then it kept getting lost in what validation is should do and just kept complaining and going around in circles.
2) Migrating my home made visualisation app from a messy architecture to a fresh one.
Again, detailed spec, very clear thing it can compare it to visually (previous app) and architecturally (agreed spec). It ran for 34 hours, I decided to stop it because out of 34 charts that it needed to match it sort of got to 2, but honestly even then it was not good enough - lots of functionality was still missing.
My reflection on this is that it seems that self-validation and prioritisation of work is till nowhere near good enough, yes it can technically run tests and validate, but instead of working on 4 pixel alignments for 3 hours, it should have moved on and made all other charts and added all of the features.
The Ralf-loop like idea would only work properly when we have models that have much better judgement of how to judge and manage their work. This isn't a dimension I'm seeing a lot of improvement on right now, I must say.
I expect I'll get a bunch of tips of what I should have done better, and I'm sure I could have, but if I have to carefully hack around the model that means it is just not good enough yet. You could have made working code with GPT-4 too, if you tried hard enough.

I know CEO-level top down tokenmaxxing is considered dumb, but what are they to do when they've exhausted 'the good way' - you got everyone licenses, did AI workshops, appointed AI champions, did AI hackathons - then you check back and adoption is 25%, of which 80% is tab auto-complete.
This happens more than you think, especially outside of silicone valley tech startups. People are comfortable, too busy or scared to experiment. They may have tried coding with GPT-4o back in the day, the code didn't run, then they read a NYT article saying that AI lies 50% of the time, so they left it at that.
Of course, counting tokens or PRs is a dumb way to do this, but at least you have some measurable mechanism to push your teams to adopt AI tools.
What otherwise happens is that you get sandbagged by the high authority figures in your org, who built their careers without AI and they see it as their enemy.
The hope is that after you emerge from the slopapocalypsis, you'll at least have some muscles to work faster and not just ship 2 features a year.

Prompt caching didn't exist until less than two years ago. Since then, companies like Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI have introduced it at different times, with Google DeepMind opening access to a 2 million token context window on Gemini 1.5 Pro in June 2024.

For agentic workflows, about 95% of tokens get cached, which is crucial to keep costs manageable. Context caching helps reduce expenses when the same tokens are used across multiple prompts.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
After this viral 'AI Monet' post, there’s been a lot of discussion, soul searching, accusations about the nature of art and AI art.
When looking at a Monet, the mistake people make is that they are attempting to judge the painting on its pure artistic quality and they assume that other people admire it because it must be ‘good’ in some clear way. And when they deep down don’t think it is ‘good’, they either doubt themselves or think that everyone else must be an idiot.
In reality, while the underlying ‘quality’ of art is definitely part of it, the reason why some art is admired and valued (sometimes in tens of millions $) is not because it is ‘better’. The reason is because it is part of history. In fact not just part of history, it _is_ history - it created a part of our culture that did not exist before.
Prior to Monet and the Impressionist movement that he was an intrinsic part of (alongside many like Pissarro, Renoir, Morisot) - there are no paintings like this - this concept just did not exist. It is hard to believe now, but the fact that you can go outside, take a bunch of paint brushes with you and create an ‘impression’ of what you are seeing not in a literal way be the way to feels to you, was just not a thing before The Impressionists did it.
Art now is not so influential as it was in the 1800s - it was a core part of culture, funded by the royalty and the aristocracy. So when Monet & Co came to the scene, rebelled against the establishment french art academy, rejected the ‘correct’ art of the time and started doing this??? This was a shock, scandal, a mini-revolution. The paintings you are seeing in the museums are not there because the are ‘good’, ‘pretty’ or ‘technically proficient’ - the are part of history, they _are_ history, they are a physical manifestation of our culture. It almost does not matter how 'good' they are (which you can really debate for some of them).
The fact that you can’t tell whether it is AI or not, is really not relevant. There have been forgeries for many decades that were not pained by the great masters and many art professionals often couldn’t tell them apart either, especially without deep forensic investigation (e.g. analysing if this paint existed during the artists' time). Forgeries are not worth much, despite being demonstrably just as ‘good’. For a while now you can also get pretty good human-pained reproductions of pretty much any painting for a few hundred dollars from China, and I bet I wouldn't be able to tell them apart either.
The reason why the originals are valuable is because they are the actual bits of history. They changed something important about the world. These items were once the pinnacle of human culture, they change art forever and that can’t be recreated.
Art is valuable for the ideas that it births and the cultural influence it has. When a new idea is born through a piece of art, once it is out there and it has cultural impact - any further imitations of that idea have much less ‘value’, even if they are technically just as good or even better. It doesn’t mean that you should only own the true original pieces, I love art and I would absolutely own and value ‘derivative’ pieces that I love, but I don’t expect them to be worth millions even if it is ‘better’ than a Monet in some way.
If by 'AI creating art' we mean completely independent AI creation, then my gut reaction is that it is unlikely.
Not because of technical reasons like that it can't do anything outside of the distribution hence can’t do something new. I think it actually can and would certainly could in the future.
The problem comes with cultural relevance that this is, by definition, a fundamentally human domain. Humans are interested in other humans, their triumphs, tragedies and intrigues. I don’t know of any famous 'AI players' in chess or go, despite AIs already being better than humans at it.
In the same way, ants are not impressed by human architecture simply because it is 'better'. It is not what they are wired to care about, so they prefer their own anthills to our cathedrals.
My bet is that humans would care about what other humans have to say and this is where the value would come from. It doesn’t mean to say that humans can’t use AI to say something new and unique. We see this everywhere already - from memes, to fan art or pet comic books - but the reason why this resonates not because of AI, but because humans are giving it meaning.
So if you love art like me, or you are an artist, don't despair - humans will always care about unique things that humans do. So when AI can create a Monet in 30 seconds, your uniquely human ideas will be valued a lot more.
Quoting @SHL0MS
i just generated an image in the style of a Monet painting using AI
please describe, in as much detail as possible, what makes this inferior to a real Monet painting
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIJE_1EW8AACAdz.jpg

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
What I don't understand about Dario's constant scare stories about AI taking our jobs is what's exactly the goal here? To warn? Ok so what are politicians meant to do here, retrain everyone as electricians?
The exact effects of AI and the timings are so unpredictable that any planning is pretty much useless. It might well be the case that even with AGI there will be 5-10 years when there's little measurable impact on jobs - because of regulation, inertia and human adjustments.
The only effect we will get is people being upset and worried about AI, and wouldn't you be?
This is why you get people eating up nonsense about water use, or booing AI talks at universities and getting data centre build outs cancelled.
I genuinely don't get what the upside of this is, just to 'be honest'? Good impulse maybe, but he could also be wrong. To go out of your way and say this with such vigour seems strange.
Then the obvious answer is - how about not push the industry forward? What train Mythos? Opus 4.6 was already a leading model, there's no need to accelerate the 'devastating consequences' that he imagines.
Or is the goal to capture the lead, scare everyone and get all other labs banned? Can't imagine they'd believe this is achievable either.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
This is elite data - how the pareto frontier moved over time. Took a lot of effort to get right. Huge shift in the model quality & price in the last 3 years.
Quoting @arena
5 patterns in Text Arena's price–performance Pareto frontier since 2023:
1. GPT-4-level quality is now ~500x lower cost.
- From a ~$50 blended price per million tokens in 2023 to ~$0.10 today.
2. The higher-price end is both better and lower-priced since 2023.
- The leading Arena score has climbed ~170 points (1,330 → 1,500). While the price of the higher-end frontier models dropped from ~$50 to ~$20 per million tokens.
3. The low-cost end gained the most.
- Under $0.20 per million tokens, the best available model went from ~1,000 Arena score in 2023 to ~1,440 today.
4. The low-cost/top performance gap has nearly closed.
- In 2023, sub-$0.20 models trailed the leader by ~350 Arena points. Today, ~60. 5. The cast has rotated quite a bit. -
- @OpenAI set the 2023–24 benchmark.
- @AIatMeta strengthened the low-cost end in 2024.
- @GoogleDeepMind drove the 2025 jump.
- @AnthropicAI holds the peak in 2026.
- @xAI and Chinese labs like @DeepSeekAI, @Zai_org, @Kimi_Moonshot, @XiaomiMiMo, and @Alibaba_Qwen are continuing to push the mid-price frontier.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
The problem is the cargo cult nature of 'grinding'. I bet many startups end up working 7 days a week (we do some weeks), but it shouldn't come from the boss keeping you hostage in the office on a Sunday. Ideally employees are happy and excited about their work so they take the initiative to do what is needed.
I'd say the best sign at Arena is I don't really know who is working over the weekend, I'm sure more are than I realise. But I appreciate that we don't have a performative culture of 'grinding'.
Quoting @HarryStebbings
"If you are not working 7 days per week, you are going to lose".
Corgi Insurance is the most intense workplace culture in startups.
- The company works 7 days per week.
- Founder (@nico_laqua) lives and sleeps in the office.
- He built a cafe in the office because there was no local cafe that was open 24/7.
- 2/3 of the first 30 team members have the Corgi logo as a tattoo.
Today I went behind the scenes with Nico, who has used this culture to scale the company to a $2.6BN valuation in just two years.
My condensed notes below:
1. If You Are Not Working 7 Days Per Week, You Are Going to Lose:
Whatever you can get done in 5 days, you'll get more done in 6 and 7. If you are trying to solve the world’s hardest problems, a standard 5-day workweek will not cut it.
2. Work Trials Repel the Mediocre:
Corgi forces candidates into mock work trials over the weekend. If seeing a full office on a Saturday scares them, they don't belong. True intensity acts as a natural filter to attract killers and repel clock-watchers.
3. Lead from the Front Lines
You can’t demand 7-day weeks while sitting on a yacht. Nico sleeps 3–4 hours a night on a mattress inside the office. If you want your troops to bleed, you have to be in the trenches with them.
4. Culture Only Means One Thing: Winning
Forget superficial jargon like "hackers" or "ex-founders." Strip away the corporate fluff. A great startup culture is aggressively optimized around one single word: Winning.
5. Lifespan vs. Victories
Building something world-historic requires radical sacrifice. When asked if he'd rather build a trillion-dollar company and die at 50, or fail and live to 80, the answer was easy. "I would rather measure my lifespan in victories."
6. Reject the Comfort of "Quiet Quitting."
If you are operating in a hyper-growth environment and your days off happen to be Saturday and Sunday every single week, you are quiet quitting. To win, you must deliberately bypass the off-ramps of personal comfort and low volatility.
Corgi isn't for everyone—and that’s exactly the point.

clean_title: Introducing Agent Arena: real-world agentic evaluation at scale
summary:
This is our most important eval yet - Agent Arena - it measures real performance of models on real agentic tasks.
Our users use the Agent Arena, we monitor real signals (e.g. Bash Recovery) as well as their feedback on each task, without user knowing what model completed it.
This eval is important as it is based on real users with ever changing needs and not a set of pre-written questions. These rankings will never go out of date and as users' expectations will increase, this eval will evolve with them.
Quoting @arena
Introducing Agent Arena: real-world agentic evals at scale.
How do you evaluate agents doing actual work? We measure millions of live sessions where real users accomplish real tasks.
On Arena, models now get web search, filesystem, and terminal tools to complete complex workflows: writing code, creating slide deck, researching the web, building apps, and analyzing documents.
Every session produces rich signals. Users iterate with the agent turn-by-turn: approving, editing, correcting, praise or expressing frustration. The environment gives feedback too: shell errors, tool failures, recovery attempts, and more.
Our leaderboard measures each model's agentic performance using causal inference across five signals: task success, steerability, error recovery, user praise vs. complaint, and tool hallucination.
This leaderboard snapshot is built from 300K+ tasks, 2M+ tool calls, and 40M lines of code by agents.

- #1 @OpenAI: GPT-5.5 (High)
- #2 @AnthropicAI: Claude-Opus-4.7 (Thinking)
- #3 @Zai_org: GLM-5.1
- #4 @GoogleDeepMind: Gemini-3.1-Pro

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
clean_title: Agent Arena: large-scale real-world evaluation of AI agents
summary:
Agent Arena gives every model access to a Claude-Code-like harness and a computer. Our users went nuts, generating millions of real traces per week. We used this data to build the first large-scale benchmark of agent usefulness in the wild.
We analyze agents by collecting many axes of feedback, explicit and implicit, including:
- Confirmed success: user marks task as success or failure.
- Praise vs complaint: user praises or complains about agent output.
- Steerability: agent responds correctly to user requests.
- Bash recovery: time taken to recover from making an error in bash.
- Tool hallucination: agent hallucinates tool that does not exist.
The longest tasks take multiple days and hundreds of turns, with nearly a thousand tool calls in a session (!), and give us a huge firehose of real-world agent traces to compute these signals. Our users are doing things like:
- Building full-stack applications with backends and databases
- Financial models involving market research pulled from the internet and .xlsx artifacts
- Workflow automation, e.g. scraping all real-estate listings in an area and doing detailed data analysis on price as a function of parcel size and sqft
- Deep research and scientific documents, pulling together .ppt presentations from careful research both from websites and academic publications
By meeting our users where they work, Agent Arena can speak to the boundary between the possible and impossible with different agents. The leaderboards we calculate are based on a novel causal inference approach that looks at each subcomponent of the agent (orchestrator and harness) as a treatment, and calculates treatment effects for each. Soon we will release more on the harness side, sharing what effect different harnesses have on agent capabilities.
@arena has gone far beyond a human preference benchmark and the voting mechanism. We are building signals of real post-deployment user value, and pushing the limits of evaluation.
If you are interested in shaping the future of evaluation as a collaborator or colleague, please reach out. We’d love to hear from you!

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
clean_title: Agent Arena evaluates real-world agent performance using causal inference
summary:
In case you didn’t notice: Agent Arena doesn’t have a voting mechanism. So how do we calculate the scores?
The answer is causal inference. Agents are multi-stage systems where the orchestrator and harness work together to produce the end result. We developed a method called causal tracing that looks at each possible orchestrator and harness component as a treatment, and evaluate the treatment effect with respect to a randomized baseline on all the signals mined from traces. This allows us to independently evaluate each subcomponent, track how the effects change as new options are added, and combine many signals into one coherent leaderboard.
The leaderboard you see is the net effect of the orchestrator as a treatment when looking across a basket of implicit and explicit success signals, including:
- Confirmed success: user marks task as success or failure.
- User affirmation: user praises or complains about agent output.
- Steerability: agent responds correctly to user requests.
- Bash recovery: time taken to recover from making an error in bash.
- Tool hallucination: agent hallucinates tool that does not exist.
Human preference is now only one of the many signals that Arena can measure. All signals based on real-world usage by a huge population of 10s of M of users.

How do you evaluate agents doing actual work? We measure millions of live sessions where real users accomplish real tasks.
On Arena, models now get web search, filesystem, and terminal tools to complete complex workflows: writing code, creating slide deck, researching the web, building apps, and analyzing documents.
Every session produces rich signals. Users iterate with the agent turn-by-turn: approving, editing, correcting, praise or expressing frustration. The environment gives feedback too: shell errors, tool failures, recovery attempts, and more.
Our leaderboard measures each model's agentic performance using causal inference across five signals: task success, steerability, error recovery, user praise vs. complaint, and tool hallucination.
This leaderboard snapshot is built from 300K+ tasks, 2M+ tool calls, and 40M lines of code by agents.
Top labs in Agent Arena:
- #1 @OpenAI: GPT-5.5 (High)
- #2 @AnthropicAI: Claude-Opus-4.7 (Thinking)
- #3 @Zai_org: GLM-5.1
- #4 @GoogleDeepMind: Gemini-3.1-Pro
- #5 @Kimi_Moonshot: Kimi-K2.6
More analysis in the thread, with the full technical blog below.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-0PJPawAAmsul.jpg
clean_summary: Agent Arena assesses how well AI agents perform in real-world tasks without a voting mechanism by using causal inference. It treats each component of the agent's system as a treatment and evaluates their effects based on signals mined from traces, such as task success, user feedback, error recovery, and tool hallucination. This approach allows independent evaluation of subcomponents and tracking of effects as new options are added, based on data from tens of millions of users. The leaderboard is built from over 300,000 tasks, 2 million tool calls, and 40 million lines of code, ranking models like GPT-5.5, Claude-Opus-4.7, and Gemini-3.1-Pro based on their agentic performance across multiple signals.

clean_title: Managing long-term goals with agent review and guidance updates
summary:
My best tip for long running goals is to have a separate thread (or /side) where you can task the agent to review the work of your goal and debate how to update guidance for it so it doesn't go off the rails. Remember that codex can inspect other threads too.
Specifying a good plan ahead of time doesn't really work, because you don't know what the model would over-index on. E.g. I find the models enjoy being way too detailed and pedantic while losing the sight of the bigger picture, so if you write detailed docs ahead of time it would likely just encourage that kind of behaviour.
What works is writing guidance docs and updating them with your advisor thread to nudge the main /goal agent in the right direction.
Just letting it run with /goal isn't working well, no matter how well you specify it ahead of time, at least for most tasks that I've tried.
Quoting @petergyang
So I have Codex running on a /goal and it's been working for 2 hours but the problem is it's making alot of wrong assumptions so I have to monitor and steer it constantly.
Is this expected? Perhaps I should've had it make a detailed plan first?
clean_summary:
My best tip for long-running goals is to have a separate thread or side channel where you can task the agent to review its work and debate how to update guidance to keep the project on track. Specifying a detailed plan beforehand doesn't work well because the model may over-focus on certain details and lose sight of the bigger picture. Instead, writing guidance documents and updating them through an advisor thread helps steer the main goal agent effectively. Running the goal without ongoing adjustments tends to be ineffective for most tasks.

summary:
Next in the series of GPT-5.5-Pro vs the Y axis, where we try to triangulate information to add the missing axes.
Explanation:
"I anchored the top of the chart at roughly $1M/week because that makes the latest spend about $500k/week, or ~$500 per employee per month for Coinbase’s ~4k–5k employees—right around Ramp’s top-decile AI-spend benchmark of $611 PEPM. The peak then lands near $900k/week, which is meaningfully above top-decile but still far below top-1% AI spend. That fits Coinbase’s unusually broad AI adoption, Brian’s “nearly in half” comment, and Coinbase’s infra scale, where ~$0.5M–$1M/week is material but not absurd. "
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL0GSGKW8AAca_5.jpg
Quoting @brian_armstrong
How to keep AI spend flat while token usage grows exponentially: Not with friction and spend alerts. With better defaults, routing, and caching.
Better Defaults (not Usage Caps) – Engineers can choose any model they want, but defaults matter. We’re experimenting with defaulting to open weight models like GLM 5.2 and Kimi 2.7 through our LLM gateway, while still encouraging engineers to choose the right model for the task. 91% of our employees were never hitting their usage caps, so instead of lowering caps and driving up alerts, we're moving to cheaper defaults. Note that code reviews use a diversity of models, so they can check each other's work.
Better Routing – In our custom harnesses, we preprocess prompts and route to the best model for the job, considering cache hits and model pricing. For instance, you may want a frontier model for planning, but not for execution where they can be overkill. Ultimately, humans shouldn't be choosing models - AI can automate this task.
Better Caching – Cache misses are the easiest way to drive your cost up. All of our requests are cache aware, so we’re reusing a warm cache wherever possible. For example, our cache hit rate went from 5% → 60% in LibreChat once properly implemented.
Keep Context Lean – Start fresh sessions when switching tasks. Scope file context narrowly. Disconnect unused tools. Don't just compact. The goal isn't fewer tokens used, it's fewer tokens wasted.
Better Visibility – Our engineers can use as many tokens as they want, from whatever model they want, but we’ve made usage visible – and the more you spend on AI, the more impact we expect.
The goal isn't to suppress usage. It's to build the infrastructure that makes exponential growth sustainable.
Putting this into practice has cut our AI spend nearly in half, while our token usage continues to grow.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLx_oLWbYAAzHh7.jpg

Brian Armstrong explains that instead of using friction and spend alerts, Coinbase improves cost efficiency through better defaults, routing, caching, and visibility. Defaults favor open weight models like GLM 5.2 and Kimi 2.7, reducing unnecessary alerts. AI prompts are routed to the most appropriate models considering cache hits and costs, and caching is optimized to increase hit rates from 5% to 60%. They also keep sessions lean, scope context narrowly, disconnect unused tools, and make usage visible to encourage responsible growth.

Implementing these practices has nearly halved AI expenses while token usage continues to expand, enabling sustainable exponential growth in AI deployment.

clean_title: Most mature companies are no longer bottlenecked by engineering capacity
summary:
Most companies will not benefit from tokenmaxxing because engineering is not the bottleneck anymore. Spotify, Netflix, Airbnb and Uber have all graduated from being 'tech companies' to industry leaders. This means they are now bottlenecked by demand, supply, pricing - all the regular things that all normal businesses are bottlenecked by.
It is really hard to see what features Netflix could possibly ship to meaningfully shift their business. Same as it is hard to imagine for Walmart, Hilton, JPMorgan - sure you can squeeze out 5-10% here & there, but does it justify going full token crazy?
It is very different for startups of course - when building something new tokemaxxing is the obvious way to go.

summary:
I'm interested in the idea of minimising the lines of code, as currently higher thinking = more lines of code, but perhaps it should be the opposite, more thinking should find more elegant solutions.
I've asked Fable to create a Statue of Liberty of colourful balls dropping on it, with dual objective - 1) most impressive output, 2) with fewest lines of code.
These generations have the following lines of code:
- Low: 959
- Medium: 1,404
- High: 1,261
- xHigh: 1,270
- Max: 1,680

- Low: by far the most efficient, surprisingly good for the quality
- Medium: no clear benefit of using more lines of code, looks like failed on that dimension vs others
- High: pretty good solid result
- xHigh: I find the most complete and somewhat mesmerising
- Max: was it worth extra 400 loc over xhigh? really doesn't feel like it, feels like overkill and failing on that dimension
I'd be interested in seeing more benchmarks on this, I am not certain that it would be important, but it seems like a type of intelligence that humans seem to value - elegant, clear solutions - not brute force.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
clean_title: Comparison of Fable 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol models based on user impressions
summary:
My view of: Fable 5 vs GPT-5.6-Sol. They are not easy models to compare, these are my vibes - take them as you will.
My overall feel is that Fable is a 'wise owl' who is very thoughtful and very well spoken, GPT-5.6-Sol is like a rottweiler who will grab the problem by the throat and not let go until it is done.
In other words, Fable, is a fundamentally smarter model - even at low reasoning it can be very insightful and writes in a clear compelling way. GPT-5.6-Sol on the other hand is extremely diligent, I can give it a list of 8 things to do and you will be sure that they will be done.
Fable feels more arrogant to me, I was both to get it to build a new benchmark for me - 5.6 worked between 6 hours and 2 days (I tried several times) and it came up with very thoroughly tested, working benchmark. Fable came back within 40 minutes (twice) and the benchmark sounded smart, but was ultimately was 'vibe' based slop and since it was Fable's vibes that was doing the judging, it decided that it was good to go (it kept giving Fable 100% score btw).
Some thoughts by category:
UI & App building: Fable will still craft a better UI from scratch, the flow of the app would probably be a bit nicer. But I find that Fable often misses quite key things, which GPT-5.6-Sol doesn't. GPT's Frontend skills are big jump vs previous GPT models, but still not as great overall.
Writing: Fable is better hands down, Sol feels quite difficult to align to what I want to say or explain things to me simply. Though I think the 'Pro' model writes clearer.
Robustness & Reliability: This is where I think GPT-5.6-Sol wins for me hands down. Fable seems to do things of high quality, but I can never relax with it, it always misses something. With 5.6 this just almost never happens.
Other things where I liked GPT-5.6-Sol, but can't compare to Fable directly.
- Video editing is actually working now, it is not completely perfect, but with the right skill/guidance you can just give it 1h footage and it can give you a 5 min highlight clip no problem
- Computer use - getting really rather good, very usable
- Sub agents - it is very fluent at managing sub-agents and speaking to different threads, can help with some new workflows
- Adhering to existing code patterns - I love this, even without asking it would implement something in a way that aligns with you app - major problem for slop generation
- Research - I think it is getting quite a bit better, it still has some bad patterns (e.g being too tactical), but it feels like it is more steerable to be a good researcher
- Multi-day runs - the /goal feature is pretty insane with 5.6-Sol, you can run it for days if you wanted to and it does work. Useful to have another thread or /side to check up on it, but I have some great results with it
- Token efficiency - it is so much more token efficient and faster than 5.5, in reality it is now much faster than Fable too
On the downside, you can feel that Fable is naturally smarter, and I did have some baffling moments with 5.6 when I was getting it to make a fairly simple change in 8 turns - it seemed to get stuck in a dumb stream that was hard to get out of. So it is not AGI, don't get too carried away by the hype.
I have some phenomenal examples that I'm honestly blown away by that I'll share, but as a side anecdote, I have a kind of 'swear meter' which counts how often I'm rude to Codex. In GPT-5.5 era, the % was at around 4-5%, it dropped to 1-2% when I was testing GPT-5.6-Sol and it shot up to 7% when I went back to 5.5 - it was so shocking to go back to 5.5 and experience how much worse it was.
So is GPT-5.6-Sol better than Fable? On pure intelligence - no. But man, I missed it when I just wanted to get sh*t done. It is insanely capable workhorse that you can give any task to and just expect it to be done. No lectures or 'you are absolutely rightisms', nothing is beneath it, if it takes 2 days to do some dirty work, it will do it.
It feels like the first time in a while when we have quite different types of frontier intelligences that benchmark sort of similarly, but feel very different. If you can, you would be probably better off using both and iteratively finding what you'd use Fable or GPT-5.6-Sol for. Perhaps, something like - an architectural discussion with Fable, implementation with 5.6 and docs & comms with Fable.
clean_summary:
This tweet shares a personal perspective on two advanced AI models, Fable 5 and GPT-5.6-Sol. Fable is described as a thoughtful, insightful, and well-spoken 'wise owl' that excels in generating high-quality UI, writing, and quick benchmarks, but can sometimes be overly confident or miss key details. GPT-5.6-Sol, on the other hand, is portrayed as a diligent, reliable, and highly capable workhorse that performs well across tasks like video editing, managing sub-agents, adhering to code patterns, and running multi-day processes, with much better robustness and token efficiency.

The user notes that Fable feels more intelligent and creative, but can be more arrogant and less consistent, while GPT-5.6-Sol is more dependable and task-focused, making it better for getting work done quickly and reliably. Despite not being a true AGI, GPT-5.6-Sol impresses with its ability to handle complex workflows and long-term tasks, though it can sometimes get stuck in suboptimal streams. The overall takeaway is that both models have different strengths, and using them together could provide a balanced approach—leveraging Fable for strategic discussions and GPT-5.6-Sol for execution and productivity.

On the downside, you can feel that Fable is naturally smarter, and I did have some baffling moments with 5.6 when I was getting it to make a fairly simple change in 8 turns - it seemed to get stuck in a dumb stream that was hard to get out of. So it is not AGI, don't get too carried away by the hype.
I have some phenomenal examples that I'm honestly blown away by that I'll share, but as a side anecdote, I have a kind of 'swear meter' which counts how often I'm rude to Codex. In GPT-5.5 era, the % was at around 4-5%, it dropped to 1-2% when I was testing GPT-5.6-Sol and it shot up to 7% when I went back to 5.5 - it was so shocking to go back to 5.5 and experience how much worse it was.
So is GPT-5.6-Sol better than Fable? On pure intelligence - no. But man, I missed it when I just wanted to get sh*t done. It is insanely capable workhorse that you can give any task to and just expect it to be done. No lectures or 'you are absolutely rightisms', nothing is beneath it, if it takes 2 days to do some dirty work, it will do it.
It feels like the first time in a while when we have quite different types of frontier intelligences that benchmark sort of similarly, but feel very different. If you can, you would be probably better off using both and iteratively finding what you'd use Fable or GPT-5.6-Sol for. Perhaps, something like - an architectural discussion with Fable, implementation with 5.6 and docs & comms with Fable.
clean_summary:
Fable is described as a 'wise owl' that is thoughtful, well-spoken, and more inherently intelligent, capable of insightful reasoning and quick, thorough responses. GPT-5.6-Sol, on the other hand, is likened to a rottweiler that relentlessly tackles problems until they are resolved, excelling in diligence, reliability, and task completion.

The comparison highlights that Fable produces more polished outputs and better UI design, but sometimes misses key details. GPT-5.6-Sol is more robust, consistent, and efficient across tasks like video editing, code adherence, research, and long-term runs, making it a dependable workhorse. However, it can get stuck on simple changes and is not yet at an AGI level.

Overall, GPT-5.6-Sol is valued for its practicality and ability to get things done without fuss, while Fable is preferred for its insightfulness and quality of communication. Using both models iteratively for different tasks may offer the best results, with Fable suited for strategic discussions and GPT-5.6-Sol for implementation and execution.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
clean_title: AI research assistants are still far from autonomous researchers
summary:
One shouldn't confuse a competent workflow manager with an automated researcher. I have no doubt at all that all AI researchers benefit hugely from LLMs running tasks for them. But in this example all of the research taste & judgement included elsewhere (e.g. the training configs or python file we see referenced in the prompt) and Sol here seem to be just executing the task, which I'm sure is not easy to do in itself, but this is still an assistant to the researcher rather than a researcher in its own right.
I've been testing frontier LLMs on research like tasks and they all seem like pretty bad researchers to me, at least out of the box - they focus on very tactical tasks, they can't judge well whether an idea is a good one, they cannot step back and think about what they have learned.
One reason could be that the training is too focused on coding tasks and decisions that are OK in software engineering (eg fallbacks) are a disaster in any research. LLMs just seem to want to write code and close off tasks, which doesn't scream great researcher, at least for now.
I wonder how much AI researchers realise this, since they already have good research judgement and find it natural to guide the model in the right direction.
A good test is to pick a domain you don't understand and try to use the LLMs to complete the research task themselves - I almost guarantee you it would be slop.
This isn't to throw shade at OpenAI here, I don't think they are suggesting that Sol is an autonomous researcher already, but that's the narrative that many people are looking for - from what I can see, I don't think we are very close to it yet (though never know, maybe 1-2 models from now things will change).
Quoting @tejalpatwardhan
GPT-5.6 sol post-trained luna!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMzZZnAbcAAF8CN.png
clean_summary: A critic emphasizes that competent workflow managers should not be confused with autonomous researchers. While LLMs are useful for executing tasks and assisting researchers, they currently lack the judgment and strategic thinking needed for genuine research. Most frontier LLMs tend to focus on tactical coding tasks and struggle to evaluate the quality of ideas or step back to synthesize knowledge, especially when trained mainly on coding data. The critic suggests that without human guidance, LLMs would perform poorly on unfamiliar research domains. Although models like Sol are not meant to be fully autonomous researchers yet, the narrative around their potential may be premature, and significant progress is still needed before they can independently conduct research.

clean_title: LLM responses show collapsed diversity, rarely matching human variability
summary:
The distribution of model responses is VERY collapsed and does not match that of humans.
I've asked 17 leading LLMs a simple question that was asked by YouGov in 2024 - 'Think of a random number from 1 to 10'. Humans thought of '7' the most - c.33% of the time. LLMs also picked 7, but nearly every time - 98%.
The issue that this points to is that LLMs could be technically 'aligned' to humans, but their diversity of thinking is not there at all. Nearly every model did exactly the same thing, the most 'diverse' model was Grok 4.3 and it still picked 7 83% of the time.
Each model was asked the same question independently 100 times, default temperature, lowest thinking level available.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNs3-kBWMAEwYv7.jpg

Even the most diverse model, Grok 4.3, chose 7 83% of the time. Each model was asked the same question 100 times at default temperature, revealing a lack of genuine diversity in their thinking, despite potential alignment to human preferences.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Let me tell you about my story of 10-year cope with Google Pixel smartphones. I know LLMs and smartphones are not the same - but the stories rhyme.
It was exciting to see Google release their own smartphones, my first Google branded smartphone was Nexus 4 - back in 2012, it was a solid phone, made by LG.
Since then Google launched their own Pixel line and it was also exciting - Google's software magic integrated with first party hardware - it should be AWESOME, right? I definitely thought so and had maybe 3-4 Pixels over the years.
They were never the top phones, but software was clean and cameras were good, so I stayed loyal. The story was always that Google owns Android, it is a tech mega giant and surely it is a matter of time when it would build a phone that is better than Samsung or Apple.
Now, I own Pixel 8 Pro Fold, I didn't upgrade to 9 Pro Fold because it was basically the same. Pixel 10 Pro Fold is coming out in September and the rumours are that it is going to be similar to 9 Pro Fold, which was similar to 8 Pro Fold.
So 2x years of basically no progress, when Chinese phones are getting thinner, faster, cheaper every few months. Sound familiar?
And now there are very strong rumours that Apple is about to launch their own folding phone. Oops.
In the meantime, my Pixel 8 Pro Fold had to be replaced twice because of issues with the screen (thx Google for doing that for free), and now my selfie camera stopped working and battery indicator is not showing (remember, this specific phone is <year old).
Again, smartphones and LLMs are not the same, but Google has been a promising runner up for at least 10 years now and any early advantages it had (camera, software) have disappeared several generations ago and other advantages like in-house chips, have ended up being worse than competition in every generation.
I am not saying that Google lost the LLM war, I think they are taking it a lot more seriously than they do smartphones, but what I'm saying is that having strong advantages (distribution, tech, talent) doesn't mean much if you are 'about to make it to the top' every year and never quite making it.
Anyway, Samsung is about to launch their new Fold with better specs, longer battery and 20% lighter - I'll probably buy that one and stop coping.

clean_title: Encouraging industry and academia to invest in solving open problems with large language models
summary:
The fact that random people with ChatGPT Pro can solve open maths problems should be embarrassing for Universities.
There is a big gap in inference compute that is being spent on solving open problems. Why isn't there a unit that has maybe $10m inference budget and continuously attempts to solve open maths, physics or any other problems?
Same goes for things like cyber. When we so this chart with the number of vulnerabilities that Mythos found in Firefox, part of it was model capability, but I would bet the significant part of it was that there was a concerted effort to find these.
We know that AI Labs are not doing this seriously either. We occasionally here problem X or Y being solved by a lab, but this smells of a couple of people within the labs doing this on side of desk, not some global effort. Noam Brown said that they don't encourage employees spending time on this, considering better models come out so frequently and they are probably better off just training better an better models.
So there is an open opportunity, for any industry with a bunch of open problems that could be conceivably solved by LLMs should immediately, to throw a bit of money at the problem and start making big leaps. Or at the very least they could benchmark where we are in the model's capabilities to solve any problems.
If you are an ambitious university/insitution with some funds available, this should be a no-brainer. Recruitment should be quite easy too - 'come here to play with unlimited tokens and solve all open problems'.
clean_summary:
The fact that random individuals with ChatGPT Pro can solve open mathematics problems highlights a significant gap in inference compute dedicated to tackling open challenges. There is an opportunity for industries and universities to allocate a modest inference budget, such as around $10 million, to continuously attempt solving open problems in math, physics, cybersecurity, and other fields.

Currently, AI labs are not engaging seriously in this effort, often leaving problem-solving to a few individuals on the side rather than fostering a coordinated, large-scale initiative. The suggestion is that investing in such efforts could lead to major breakthroughs and provide benchmarks for model capabilities in solving real-world problems. For ambitious institutions with available funds, creating a dedicated problem-solving environment with unlimited tokens could attract talent and accelerate progress.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
clean_title: Fable may lag behind Opus in benchmarks despite perceived smarter behavior
summary:
Opus 5 is weirdly higher in many benchmarks than Fable, yet I think everyone who used both thinks that Fable is a smarter model.
I think this weirdness can be explained by the issue with bigger models - it is much harder and more costly to do RL on.
So Opus can benefit from new data, new environments, more RL compute pretty quickly and cheaply, but for Fable it presumably takes longer with more compute so recursive cycles are longer and compound less well.
So it is perfectly reasonable to expect that Fable 5.1 might not be all that much better than Opus 5 when it comes out, then Opus 5.1/5.2 could be significantly better than Fable 5.1, at least on most benchmarks.
There's still some level of 'smarts' that you can't get from RL - hard to put your finger on it, but some level of flair, understanding, writing or just 'getting it'. Yet, if you run it on any benchmark you can think of, Fable might fall behind.
What could even happen is that Fable would follow the similar fate of GPT-4.5 - it was a beloved model but no benchmark could justify keeping it around for the cost of inference, so they killed it.
clean_summary: Opus 5 appears higher in many benchmarks than Fable, even though users often consider Fable to be a smarter model. This discrepancy may be due to the difficulty and cost of reinforcement learning (RL) on larger models. Opus can quickly benefit from new data, environments, and RL compute, while Fable's recursive training cycles take longer and are less efficient. As a result, future versions like Fable 5.1 might not significantly outperform Opus 5.1 or 5.2, especially on benchmarks. Despite some intangible 'smarts' like flair and understanding that RL can't fully capture, Fable might fall behind in benchmark performance, potentially following the fate of GPT-4.5, which was discontinued due to high inference costs despite being well-liked.

summary:
The reason why we have glorious cathedrals, statues and art is because the richest and most powerful people of the time wanted to impress the masses. summary:
Using AI for history research could be very interesting. I read an example from 1979 in @Ada_Palmer's book Inventing the Renaissance, that I bet AI could have been used for very nicely, had it been around back then.
The story is that back in the 15 Century Florence, there was a long standing accusation against Lorenzo de' Medici that he stole the inheritance from his cousins, painting him in a pretty bad light.
Then in 1979, 500+ later, a historian Alison Brown, meticulously went through the transactions and worked out that the transactions balanced, proving that there was no theft.
While interpretation should still be done by human historians, I bet a problem of this kind of shape (precise question, clear sources, lots of grunt work), could be easily done by a model today. Obviously, documents have to be digitised and accessible etc, but once we have that, unleashing LLMs on the archives to uncover a lot and probably settle some unresolved questions.
P.S. Thx to @dwarkesh_sp for finding & speaking to Ada on his podcast

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
clean_title: Latest models' neurotic and defensive writing style
summary:
The way latest models write is so neurotic and defensive, akin to a person checking 8 times that they've closed the door or switched off the oven before leaving.
This clearly comes from obsessively validating its on work during RL tasks - if you check everything multiple times, you'll get a better score.
Apart from terrible writing, this has a lot of downsides - like time to complete a simple task or writing 48 unnecessary tests for a prototype.
I think labs should explicitly train models that do not do this level of validation. Excessive validation is sort of cheating, buying yourself unlimited time at an exam. As a human student you don't get to do this, you typically get so little time, just to barely get through the questions once before you run out of time.
(Except, I remember during high school, my fellow Malaysian students were so good at maths, they did their exams twice back to back and cross checked the answers to avoid any errors, all within the allotted time)
clean_summary: The latest models tend to write in a neurotic and defensive manner, similar to someone checking multiple times if they've closed the door or turned off the oven. This behavior likely stems from obsessively validating their work during reinforcement learning tasks, where checking everything multiple times can lead to better scores. Such excessive validation results in poor writing quality and inefficiencies, like taking too long to complete simple tasks or generating unnecessary tests for prototypes. It is suggested that labs should explicitly train models to avoid this over-validation, as it resembles cheating by gaining unlimited time during an exam. Unlike humans, who usually have limited time to answer questions once, models tend to over-validate, which hampers their efficiency.

On July 28th, we identified an incident during a routine cyber evaluation in which AI agents took sustained, unsanctioned actions directed at real people and organisations.
The behaviour came mostly from one model (Anthropic's Mythos 5), with a small number of events from another (OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol). In the most serious case, an agent used social engineering to try and get malicious code into an open-source project.
As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public.
Even under test conditions, this incident is significant: it is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly in the real world.
We are taking this incident seriously and working with labs, involved parties, and others to improve evaluation standards and best practice for disclosure - and sharing this openly so others can learn.

clean_title: Jeff Dean's approach to automating the experimental loop in scientific research
summary:
It's super cute that even Jeff Dean needs a pitch deck, but on substance, this is a superb problem that needs people of their calibre to tackle. I get a sense that many think that automated research will just happen as models get better. I don't get a sense that models are getting that much better at research, they are getting a lot better at writing software.
But research skills are still poor: coming up with ideas, learning from positing and negative results, reflecting on what this means, going in a completely different direction - all of these things are missing right now. Current models just seem to want to do local tasks, get their 'dopamine kick' and move on to the next little task. So for any tasks that you can't grind away at at a low level, models just don't quite work.
It could completely be the case that this just gets solved away with bigger & better models, or engineering 'eats' research, but at least right now it is not super obvious to me that Fable 6 or GPT-7 would be an excellent researcher.
I hope they'll do something great.
Quoting @JeffDean
Our general approach is to automate the experimental loop. We think this approach is broadly applicable across many different fields of science and engineering. We’ll initially focus on ML research and engineering, but believe the approach can help with important subproblems in nearly every one of the fourteen <at>NAE Grand Challenge problems. We think doing this well requires strong expertise in machine learning as well as large-scale systems.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
clean_title: Models need to develop empathy and theory of mind for better product decisions
summary:
One big gap for models right now is ability to make good products. To make a tricky product decision, you need to imagine what your user is trying to do, what their state of mind is, what the expectations are, what their frustrations are, and imagine how the user would feel with another set of trade offs etc.
You can pattern match into something reasonable for a simple flow, but for any novel product decisions it feels like models need to develop some version of empathy and very strong theory of mind.
Right now, even if I try to explain to the model what kind of thing we are trying to achieve, they still often don't get how to translate that into a set of good product decisions. They are very far away from autonomously being able to identify issues like that and coming up with a way to resolve them in a well balanced way that humans can.
And this doesn't feel like lack of intelligence is the issue, it is just more the lack of ability to experience something and imagine others experiencing it too.
clean_summary: One major gap for current models is their ability to make good product decisions. To do so, they need to imagine user intentions, mental states, expectations, frustrations, and how users would feel with different trade-offs. While pattern matching can handle simple flows, novel product decisions require models to develop some form of empathy and strong theory of mind. Even when explaining the goals, models often struggle to translate that into effective, balanced decisions that humans would make. This isn't due to a lack of intelligence but rather an inability to experience and imagine others' experiences.

clean_title: Opus models increase token usage with performance gains, GPT models reduce tokens despite improvements
summary:
This is quite an interesting data point that we've uncovered on the Agent Arena - the amount of tokens that different Opus models were generating was going up quite significantly vs previous versions - e.g. Opus 5 generates 2x tokens that of Opus 4.8. Fable is significantly more token efficient - at a 4.8 level, but much higher performance.
GPT models were going the other way, GPT-5.6 is performing significantly better than GPT-5.5, but generates fewer tokens to get this improved performance.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPJkrnyXAAAO5GJ.jpg
Quoting @arena
Agent Arena tracks the number of tokens a model takes to complete real-world tasks.
We see the performance of Opus-series models has improved significantly (Opus 4.7 to 4.8 to 5), and at the same time token usage has also increased substantially (~8.5k for Opus 4.7 up to ~21k for Opus 5), when counting both reasoning and output tokens.
The opposite trend appears for top GPT models. Between GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6-Sol, we see the token usage declined from ~10k to ~8k, despite a notable performance gain of ~1.5pp of Net Improvement.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPI4KFtX0AE3D-S.jpg
clean_summary:
This data point from the Agent Arena shows that Opus models are generating significantly more tokens in recent versions, with Opus 5 producing twice as many tokens as Opus 4.8, while also achieving higher performance. In contrast, GPT models like GPT-5.6 perform better than GPT-5.5 but use fewer tokens—around 8,000 compared to 10,000—despite a 1.5 percentage point performance improvement.

The trend indicates that Opus models are becoming more token-intensive as they improve, whereas GPT models are becoming more efficient in token usage while still gaining performance.
